sentences: Before us is Sehando, Winter Scene, by the scholar Kim Jeong-hui, known by his pen name Chusa.
The picture holds just a humble house and four trees.
Everything else is empty, silent winter air.
In 1844, Kim was living in exile on Jeju Island.
When everyone else abandoned the disgraced scholar, his student Yi Sang-jeok, an interpreter, kept sending him rare books obtained in China, carried across the sea.
At the upper right are the title, Sehando, and the painter's seals.
The small line beside it reads, roughly, Useon, please enjoy this, signed with Kim's pen name Wandang; Useon was Yi's pen name.
It tells us the picture was a gift for one person.
Below the title stands an old pine.
Its trunk is bent and it has almost no needles left, a tree that has endured many years.
Another tree stands right beside it, holding out against the winter together.
In the middle sits the humble house, plain and simple, with a single round window and no sign of anyone inside.
Some read it as a portrait of the painter's own situation, living alone and far from home in exile.
Come closer to the lines.
They were drawn with a dry brush carrying very little ink, and you can still see where the bristles split and caught on the paper.
The lines are plain and therefore strong.
Two more trees stand to the left of the house.
Kim answered his student's loyalty with a line from Confucius: only when the year turns cold do we see that the pine and the cypress are the last to fade.
These trees carry that message for him.
To the left of the picture continues Kim's own handwritten note.
On paper ruled into a grid, in upright, disciplined script, he explains why he made the painting and thanks Yi for his books and his faithfulness.
Picture and words together become a single letter.
Yi carried the painting to Beijing, where sixteen Chinese scholars added their own colophons.
Later Korean writers added theirs too, and today the scroll stretches nearly fifteen meters.
The painting kept gathering voices long after Kim set down his brush.
The painting once belonged to the Japanese scholar Fujitsuka Chikashi.
In 1944 the calligrapher Son Jae-hyeong went to Japan and brought it home.
In 2020 Son Chang-geun donated it to the National Museum of Korea.
Now step back and look at all that empty space.
Only in the coldest season, Kim tells us, do we see what stays green.
Before you go, think for a moment: who stood by you in your own winter?
